title: The account: their cloud or your server, and what each costs
promise: You'll have n8n open and running through the path you chose, with the account set up or the installation running. You'll know exactly what you're going to pay each month and where to check that number before the bill arrives.
why: Nuria builds automations for an accounting firm. She started with n8n's cloud free trial, built four flows in two weeks, and everything was going well. On day 15 the trial ended. The flows stopped at three in the afternoon. Nobody noticed until a client called asking about an email that never arrived. It wasn't an n8n bug: nobody checked when the trial ended or what happened when it did. Half an hour of reading on day one would have prevented that afternoon.

theory.title: The three paths, and what you pay on each
theory.text: There are three ways to have n8n running and they don't compete with each other: they're for different moments. One, n8n's cloud: you pay a monthly fee and handle nothing. Two, install it on your own computer: free, turns off when you turn off your laptop, perfect for learning and testing. Three, install it on your own server: free license, a few dollars a month in server costs, and maintenance is yours. Almost everyone does path 2 while learning and then jumps to 1 or 3.
theory.analogy: Rehearsing at home, renting a space by the hour, or building your own space. All three work, just not at the same moment.

visual.title: The three paths, and which one fits you today
visual.caption: They don't compete: they're for different moments. Almost everyone starts on their own computer and later jumps to the cloud or their own server.
visual.question: What do you need RIGHT NOW, not a year from now?

branches.answer: Learn and build my first flows
branches.why: It's the same full program, nothing trimmed. Good enough to build and test all fifty lessons. When you want to move it, you export a file and that's it.

branches.answer: Have a flow actually work and not depend on my laptop
branches.why: No more maintenance, and the flow stays alive with your computer off. They bill per flow execution, not per step, so a long flow doesn't cost more than a short one.
branches.cost: Monthly fee, check it at n8n.io

branches.answer: High volume, or data that can't leave my company
branches.why: No license cost, and data stays wherever you say. In exchange, updates, backups, and a Sunday outage are yours.
branches.cost: $5-15/month for the server, plus your hours

theory.title: What the cloud bills isn't what you think
theory.text: n8n's cloud charges per flow execution, not per step. A twenty-node flow (twenty boxes) that fires a hundred times a month is a hundred executions, not two thousand. That's exactly the opposite of Zapier, and it's what makes n8n cheap on long processes. What does count separately is active flows: plans limit how many you can have turned on at once.
theory.example: Rocio's flow has four actions and fires six times a day: 180 executions a month on n8n, 720 tasks on Zapier.

visual.title: The same thing, billed two different ways
visual.caption: A 20-step flow firing 100 times a month. Look at what each one counts.

items.label: n8n on their cloud: the whole flow counts

theory.title: n8n's free tier is real, with fine print that does matter
theory.text: The version you install yourself is free and full-featured for your own use and your business's. The license is called the "sustainable use license." In plain terms: you can use it for yourself and to automate your own business or your clients' businesses. What you can't do is take n8n, slap your logo on it, and sell it as your own product. For 99% of people this changes nothing. If you're planning to build a service where your clients log into an n8n of yours, read it.
theory.analogy: A tool lent to you to work with, not to resell in your own storefront.

theory.title: Installing it on your computer isn't "the toy version"
theory.text: It's exactly the same program. The only difference is your laptop turns off and a server doesn't. Flows scheduled for eight in the morning won't fire if the computer is closed. And a webhook, the door through which other programs alert your flow, won't be able to receive alerts from outside: your computer doesn't have a public internet address. For learning, building, and testing, it's perfect and lacks nothing.
theory.example: You can build the whole flow on your laptop, test it thoroughly, export it to a file, and upload it as-is to the cloud or a server once it's ready.

visual.title: The n8n screen, by zone
visual.caption: Click each zone. These are the five you'll use; the rest can wait.

areas.name: Top bar
areas.what: The flow's name, the save button, and the activate switch. That switch is what makes the flow run on its own: tested but off does nothing.
areas.tip: Constantly forgotten. After activating, trigger the real case once and check it fired.

areas.name: Canvas
areas.what: Where you drag the boxes and connect them. It's your drawing of the process: each box does one thing and the arrows say what order.
areas.tip: The + button in the center adds the first step. Every flow starts with a trigger.

areas.name: Node panel
areas.what: The box search. Type an application's name or what you want to do and options come up.
areas.tip: You'll use six or seven of the thousand boxes there. Don't get lost in the list.

areas.name: Executions
areas.what: The history of every time the flow has run, with its status. This is where you investigate any "it didn't work."
areas.tip: Each line opens and shows what went in and out of each box. This is the screen you'll live in.

areas.name: Box data panel
areas.what: Opening a box shows three columns: what comes in on the left, configuration in the middle, and what goes out on the right.
areas.tip: Looking at the right column after running is how you really learn n8n.

theory.title: What a server of your own really costs
theory.text: A small server running n8n costs between $5 and $15 a month with any provider. What doesn't show up on that bill is the hours. Setting it up right the first time is one afternoon. After that you have to update it, back it up, and be available the day it goes down. If you automate for clients, that availability is part of what you're selling and needs to be charged for or not offered.
theory.analogy: A company car doesn't cost what's on the contract: it costs that plus the checkups, the insurance, and the mornings at the shop.

theory.title: Choosing badly now isn't serious, not choosing is
theory.text: An n8n flow exports to a file and imports into another installation in two clicks. Moving from your laptop to the cloud, or from the cloud to your server, is a matter of minutes per flow. What is costly is not deciding. For example, leaving the free trial running without checking when it ends, like Nuria. Or building on a computer someone turns off on Fridays.
theory.example: Exporting is "Download" in the flow's menu, and it downloads a JSON file (a text file with all the flow's data). Importing is dragging it onto the other installation's canvas.

visual.title: Choosing badly isn't serious. Not choosing is
visual.caption: Moving somewhere is exporting a file. The other thing is what's expensive.

rows.after: Moving from your computer to the cloud: export and import

tasks.title: Confirm your decision with the paper in front of you
tasks.action: Reread the two lines you wrote: what you're going with and why. If in the previous lesson you chose the cloud, continue with task 2. If you chose to install it yourself, continue with task 4. And if you're still unsure, start on your own computer: it's free, reversible, and what everyone does while learning.
tasks.expect: One of the three paths chosen, with its reason written down.
tasks.stuck: If you're torn between the cloud and your computer, start with your computer: you can move later by exporting a file.

tasks.title: Going with the cloud: create the account
tasks.action: Go to n8n.io and click the start button. Sign up with your work email, not a personal one. A business's automation account shouldn't hang off the Gmail you use for the grocery list. You'll get a workspace with its own address ending in app.n8n.cloud.
tasks.expect: You're in, looking at an empty canvas with a big button to add the first step.
tasks.stuck: If the confirmation email doesn't arrive in five minutes, check spam and confirm you typed the domain correctly.

tasks.title: Going with the cloud: note when the trial ends and what happens after
tasks.where: In your account menu, billing section
tasks.action: Find the exact end date of the free trial and put it on your calendar with an alert three days before. And check the pricing page for what happens once it ends: whether flows stop, data gets deleted, or it just stops letting you create more. This is what cost Nuria an afternoon.
tasks.expect: A date on your calendar and a written sentence of what happens that day.
tasks.stuck: If you can't find the date on the dashboard, check the welcome email: it's usually there.

tasks.title: Going with your computer: check what you already have installed
tasks.where: In the terminal (PowerShell on Windows, Terminal on Mac)
tasks.action: Type these two, one at a time, and press Enter: node --version and docker --version. Note what each shows. There are two ways to install n8n and each needs one of these two things; knowing what you already have saves you installing extra.
tasks.expect: Two answers: either a version number, or a message saying the command isn't recognized. Both answers are useful information.
tasks.stuck: If the terminal scares you, don't worry: type, press Enter, read. You can't break anything with those two commands.

tasks.title: Going with your computer: choose between the two ways to install
tasks.action: With Node.js installed, n8n gets set up with a single command and starts in a minute: it's the fastest way to learn. With Docker, n8n lives inside an isolated box and doesn't clutter your computer. Plus, it's exactly like how it'll run on a server: it's what's used for real. If you have Docker or don't mind installing it, go with Docker; lesson 04 walks through it step by step.
tasks.expect: One of the two chosen and written down.
tasks.stuck: If you just want to see n8n running today and decide later, go with Node: it uninstalls just as easily.

tasks.title: Start n8n for the first time
tasks.where: In the terminal, or in your browser if going with the cloud
tasks.action: The fast Node route, the command is npx n8n. It takes a couple of minutes the first time because it downloads itself, and then it tells you what address to open: usually http://localhost:5678. Open it in your browser. If going with Docker, skip to lesson 04. If going with the cloud, you're already in.
tasks.expect: n8n open in the browser, with an empty canvas and a button to add the first step.
tasks.stuck: If you get "port in use," something else is occupying 5678, almost always another n8n left open from before. Close it or start on a different port.

tasks.title: Create your user inside n8n
tasks.action: It'll ask for email, name, and password. Watch out, this is confusing: this isn't an n8n.io account, it's the user for YOUR installation, and that password isn't recoverable by email by anyone. Save it in your password manager now, not later.
tasks.expect: You're inside your own installation, with your user created.
tasks.stuck: If you lose it on a local installation, the fix is deleting n8n's data and starting from zero. Save it.

tasks.title: Set the time zone before building anything
tasks.action: Find the time zone and set it to your local one. By default many installations come set to UTC, which runs several hours off from most US time zones depending on daylight saving. If you don't fix this now, three lessons from now you'll have a flow scheduled for eight that fires at a different time and won't know why.
tasks.expect: Your local time zone saved in settings.
tasks.stuck: If you can't find the setting in your version, note it as pending: lesson 17, the one on dates, resolves it anyway.

tasks.title: Run the test that everything's alive
tasks.action: Click the button to add the first step, choose the manual trigger ("Trigger manually"), and then add any node that doesn't touch anything external; the most harmless one is the one that waits a few seconds or the one that edits fields. Click the run button and watch the boxes turn green.
tasks.expect: Two green boxes and a run showing up in the history. That tells you the installation actually works.
tasks.stuck: If it doesn't turn green, open the box and check the output tab: the error message will tell you what's missing.

tasks.title: Write down what you're going to pay
tasks.action: One line with the number: monthly fee if going with the cloud, server cost if going self-hosted, or zero if going with your computer. And next to it, where to check that number (the exact screen) and the date to review it. Data as of August 2026; prices change and this note is for you, not forever.
tasks.expect: A number, a place to check it, and a review date.
tasks.stuck: If going with your computer and the cost is zero, write zero: having the number written down, even zero, is what makes you check it.

errors.message: The trial ended and flows stopped without warning
errors.means: The free period ended. It's not a bug: it's what was written, and nobody checked it. Flows stop running, and whoever was waiting on the result finds out.
errors.fix: Calendar alert three days before the end of any free trial, and a written sentence of what happens that day. If it's already happened, check which cases went unprocessed in those hours and recover them by hand first.

errors.means: Port 5678 is already in use by another program, almost always another n8n you left open in another terminal and thought was closed.
errors.fix: Find the terminal it was running in and press Ctrl+C. If you can't find it: on Windows npx kill-port 5678, on Mac lsof -ti:5678 | xargs kill. You can also start on a different port, but you'll end up with zombie installations.

errors.message: 'n8n' is not recognized as an internal or external command
errors.means: It's not installed, or the terminal was opened before installing it and doesn't know yet.
errors.fix: Try the free fix first: close the terminal entirely and reopen it. If it persists, check Node is there with node --version; if that doesn't respond either, install it from nodejs.org, choosing the LTS version.

errors.message: I've lost my local n8n's password
errors.means: The user you created on startup lives inside your installation and there's no recovery email behind it.
errors.fix: On a local installation, the realistic way out is deleting n8n's data and starting from zero, losing whatever was inside. That's why it gets saved to the password manager the same day. If you have important flows, export them before touching anything.

errors.message: Scheduled flows don't fire at the time I set
errors.means: The time zone is set to UTC, which is what many installations ship with by default. It runs several hours off from most US time zones.
errors.fix: Settings, time zone, your local one. Then check a scheduled run by looking at the actual time it fires, not the time you think it will.

errors.message: My flow was working and it stopped when I closed my laptop
errors.means: It's not a bug: n8n installed on your computer turns off when your computer does. Scheduled flows and webhooks need something on twenty-four hours a day.
errors.fix: While you're learning, that's fine: turn it on when you're working. Once the flow needs to work for real, export the file and set it up on the cloud or a server. Covered in lesson 46.

errors.message: A webhook receives nothing even though the flow is active
errors.means: If n8n is on your computer, it has no public address: the outside service has no way to reach you.
errors.fix: For testing, n8n gives you a test address that works while the editor is open. For production, n8n needs to be somewhere with a public address. Covered in full in lesson 27.

matters: Setting the time zone to your local one on day one. It's a thirty-second setting and it's the cause of a scheduled flow firing at a time you can't understand. It drags on for weeks if not fixed at the start.
Writing down any free trial's end date, with an alert three days before. The day it ends, flows stop, and your client finds out before you do.
Saving your local installation's password to the password manager the moment you create it. There's no recovery email behind it: if it's lost, it's lost along with everything inside.
Writing down the number you're going to pay and where to check it. Even if it's zero. Having the number written down is what makes someone check it before the bill arrives.
ignore: Setting up your own server before having a working flow. It's an afternoon of work to solve a problem you don't have yet, and it's the most common way to end up three days later having automated nothing.
Advanced configuration options: external databases, queues, scaling, multiple workers. All of that exists for volumes you don't have, and the defaults hold up far more than you think.
Comparing paid plans while you're still learning. With the installation on your own computer you can build and test absolutely everything in the next forty lessons without spending a dollar.
canDo: Work exactly the same whether it's on your laptop, their cloud, or your server: it's the same program, and a flow moves from one to the other by exporting a file.
Let you build and test the whole course for free on your own computer, no card, no time limit.
Charge you per flow execution and not per step on their cloud, which is what makes it cheap on processes with many steps.
Export any flow to a file you can save, version, and reimport wherever you want.
cantDo: Run anything while your computer is off. Scheduled flows and webhooks need something on all the time, and that's no longer your laptop.
Recover a local installation's password. There's no "forgot my password" behind that.
Warn you the free trial is ending in a way you'll actually notice. An email does arrive, yes, among forty others.
Maintain itself if you install it yourself: updates, backups, and outages become yours from minute one.
words: Instance
Your specific n8n, the one you started. You can have several and they don't talk to each other.
Self-hosted
Installed on your computer or your server. No license cost, and maintenance is on you.
Cloud
The n8n they host and you rent by the month. No maintenance, less control.
Execution
Every time a whole flow runs. It's the unit the cloud bills, whether the flow has two steps or twenty.
Active flow
One that's turned on and running on its own. Plans limit how many you can have active at once.
localhost:5678
The address where n8n lives when running on your computer. It only exists for you: nobody outside can open it.
Port
The number at the end of the address. Only one program can occupy each number, hence the "port in use" error.
npx
A command that runs a program without installing it permanently. It's the fast way to try n8n today.
Time zone
The offset n8n uses to interpret times. If it's set to UTC and you're not, everything scheduled runs shifted.
Export / import
Pulling a flow out into a file and loading it into another installation. It's what makes switching places cheap.
next: If you chose Docker, lesson 04 installs it with you step by step and keeps your data safe from an accidental wipe. If you already have n8n open through the fast route, you can skip to lesson 05 and start learning the screen.
